cases.title: The Moon is drifting away
cases.intro: Lasers bounce off reflectors on the Moon. Measurements collected over many years reveal a slow outward drift hidden beneath its changing distance each month.

facts.label: Average outward drift of the orbit; published estimate with uncertainty
facts.source_name: Williams and Boggs (2016), Celestial Mechanics and Dynamical Astronomy; JPL/Caltech

facts.label: Reflector deployment years: Apollo and Soviet Luna missions
facts.source_name: International Laser Ranging Service (ILRS), hosted by NASA GSFC

facts.label: APOLLO laser-ranging record described in the paper
facts.source_name: Battat et al. (2023), APOLLO dataset characterization; Apache Point Observatory

quiz.q: Which evidence best reveals the Moon's slow outward drift?
options: Its size in a single photograph
Laser measurements collected over many years
quiz.why: The distance changes during each orbit. Long records let scientists separate those repeating changes from the slow outward drift.

cases.title: New craters still form
cases.intro: The Moon's surface keeps changing. Compare pictures of the same ground taken years apart to find fresh craters left by incoming space rocks.

facts.label: New impact craters detected in the survey, not a yearly or whole-Moon total
facts.source_name: Speyerer et al. (2016), Nature; NASA LRO/LROC observations

facts.label: Excess over the Neukum model for craters at least ten metres wide; not growth over time
facts.source_name: Speyerer et al. (2016), Nature; NASA LRO/LROC observations

facts.label: Image collection period used for the published new-crater search
facts.source_name: Watters, Speyerer and Robinson (2022), LPSC abstract 1626; LROC investigators

quiz.q: The survey found more craters than a model predicted. What does that show?
options: The Moon's impact rate must be increasing each year
Every crater on the Moon is new
The model underestimated crater formation in this survey
quiz.why: A higher count than a model predicts does not prove impacts are becoming more frequent. Before-and-after images show that new craters formed.

cases.title: Flashes reveal hidden impacts
cases.intro: Telescopes watch the Moon's unlit ground for brief flashes from space rocks hitting the surface. Clear skies and repeated observations help separate impacts from camera noise.

facts.label: Lunar impacts observed by NASA Marshall; cumulative report, not an annual rate
facts.source_name: NASA Marshall, Automated Lunar and Meteor Observatory anniversary report (2026)

facts.label: Flashes selected under clear, stable skies for the published study
facts.source_name: Suggs et al. (2014), Icarus; NASA Meteoroid Environment Office, Table 1

facts.label: Lower impact-energy limit for the study's reported flux, not a typical impact energy
facts.unit: J of estimated impact kinetic energy
facts.source_name: Suggs et al. (2014), Icarus; NASA Meteoroid Environment Office, abstract

facts.label: Telescopes used together to reject cosmic rays and camera noise
facts.source_name: NASA Meteoroid Environment Office, Lunar Impact Monitoring

quiz.q: Why watch the same flash with separate telescopes?
options: To check that it is real rather than camera noise
quiz.why: A flash seen by separate telescopes is less likely to be a cosmic ray or camera glitch. Repeated checks make the evidence stronger.

cases.title: Old records reveal Moon shakes
cases.intro: Astronauts left ground sensors on the Moon. Their recordings still hold clues: scientists can find missed shaking events by examining old data more carefully.

facts.label: Apollo seismic observation period
facts.source_name: Onodera (2024), JGR: Planets; NASA Apollo data reanalysis, corrected in 2026

facts.label: Previously identified events in long-period data; includes impacts, not just tectonic quakes
facts.source_name: Onodera (2024), JGR: Planets; NASA Apollo data reanalysis, corrected in 2026

facts.label: Newly detected events in reanalyzed short-period data; includes thermal shaking and impacts
facts.unit: new seismic-event detections in old data
facts.source_name: Onodera (2024), JGR: Planets; NASA Apollo data reanalysis, corrected in 2026

quiz.q: Why did scientists find more events after the sensors stopped working?
options: The Moon must be shaking more often today
They found missed signals in old recordings
quiz.why: Better analysis can reveal missed events in old records. A larger catalog does not show that the Moon is shaking more often today.
